opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so before Anthropic I was running a robotics company, and I was writing a lot of code myself. When I started using Copilot, it was one of those moments where it really clicked for me. At first it was just autocomplete, finishing a line here and there, but pretty quickly I noticed it was writing whole functions that were basically correct, and I started structuring how I worked around it. I'd write a comment describing what I wanted and let it fill in the rest.

What struck me wasn't just that it was useful today; it was the slope. Every few months the models got noticeably better, and if you extrapolate that even a little, you realize this is going to change almost everything about how software gets built, and probably a lot more than software. Coming from robotics, where progress is slow and gated by hardware and the physical world, it was kind of jarring to see something improving that fast in pure software.

So it shifted my thinking from "AI is a neat tool" to "this is probably the most important technology happening right now, and I want to be working on it directly." And if I was going to work on it, I wanted to be somewhere that took both the capabilities and the safety side seriously, because if it's going to be that powerful, getting it right really matters. That's a big part of what drew me to Anthropic, and specifically to working on coding, since that was where I'd personally felt the impact first.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Copilot progressed from autocomplete to writing mostly correct functions and changed his view of AI, but it never says this would have counted as AGI to him ten years earlier.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was a really pivotal moment for me. I'd been doing a robotics startup, Cobalt, for about five or six years, and I was pretty deep in the hardware world. And the thing about robotics is that progress is slow. You're fighting physics, you're fighting supply chains, you're fighting the fact that the real world is messy, and it's hard to get a tight feedback loop.

And then I started using Copilot, this was maybe late 2021, early 2022, and I remember the first time it autocompleted an entire function that I was about to write. Not a trivial one, something with some actual logic in it. And I just sat there for a second. Because I'd followed AI progress from a distance, I'd read the papers, I'd seen GPT-2 and GPT-3 demos, but demos are easy to discount. You can always tell yourself it's cherry-picked. Copilot was different because it was in my editor, doing my actual work, on my actual codebase, every day. There was no way to cherry-pick that.

And what hit me was the rate of change more than the absolute capability. It was clearly not perfect, it would hallucinate APIs that didn't exist, but I could extrapolate the curve, and the curve was steep. I think a lot of people underestimate things because they look at where something is rather than how fast it's moving. And as an engineer, I had a very visceral sense of "okay, this is going to eat a huge fraction of what I do."

So that reframed the question for me of where to spend my time. I'd been working on a problem, security robots, where I thought the impact was real but bounded. And here was this thing that looked like it was going to touch basically every knowledge worker. And I thought, if this is the most important technology of my lifetime, and I genuinely believed it might be, then the thing I want to be doing is working on it directly, and specifically working on making it go well. That's what led me to Anthropic. The safety framing mattered a lot to me, because if you believe the capabilities are coming this fast, then whether it goes well becomes the whole ballgame.

And honestly, there's a selfish component too. I just wanted to be close to it. Once you see the thing moving that fast, it's very hard to go back to working on something slower.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes Copilot completing a function and predicts AI will handle a large share of his work, but does not say AI was writing much of his code or that this would have counted as AGI to him ten years earlier.

astra-6.text:
Using Copilot was one of the first times I felt AI changing the way I worked every day. You’d start writing something, and it would finish the thought. It wasn’t always right, but it was useful often enough that you quickly got used to having it. And then, when you didn’t have it, you really noticed.

That made progress in AI feel much more concrete to me. It went from something you could read about or see in a demo to something that actually made me more productive. And coding is such an interesting case because helping people build software also helps them build the next generation of tools.

So I started thinking, if this is already useful, where does it go as the models get better? I wanted to work closer to that progress—to help build the systems behind these capabilities. That was a big part of what drew me toward working on AI directly.

r001.rationale: The response says Copilot completed thoughts and improved productivity, but it does not state that AI wrote much of Erik Schluntz’s code or that this would have counted as AGI to him ten years earlier.

sol-6.1.text:
Copilot was one of the first times I felt like AI was helping me do something I was already good at. When you’re writing code, you have a pretty good sense of what’s easy and what’s hard, so seeing a model suggest the next few lines—or occasionally a whole function—made the progress feel very concrete.

It also made me think about where this was going. If a model could help me write code, how far away were we from one that could take on a larger piece of the work? I wanted to work closer to that frontier, where improvements in the models could turn into a fundamentally different way of building software.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Copilot suggested lines or sometimes a whole function and made AI progress feel concrete, but it does not state that AI wrote much of Erik’s code or that this would have counted as AGI ten years earlier.
